video_title: The AI Boom Is Creating a Financial System We Haven't Seen Before (Paul Kedrosky Explains)
gist: Paul Kedrosky argues the AI buildout is the first US boom to sit at the intersection of every historical bubble ingredient (loose credit, a real technology story, real estate, and policy), and that as of mid-2026 more than half of data-center financing has flipped from hyperscaler cash flow to external debt (ABS, private credit, sovereigns), making data-center paper roughly 15-18% of the investment-grade market. He pairs that with a deflation trap - token prices falling 70-80% a year force frontier labs to grow ~400% just to stand still - and with evidence that model quality has flatlined and converged, so the equity, credit and semiconductor complex built on continued frontier training is structurally overdetermined to fail.

insights.claim: The current AI buildout is the first US boom to combine all four historical bubble ingredients at once - loose credit, a genuine technology story, a real-estate component, and a policy angle - which is why single-lens analyses (credit-only, real-estate-only, tech-only) keep underestimating it.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Investors modeling AI risk through one channel will miss correlated breakage; stress tests should run credit, real-estate/lease, equity and policy shocks jointly.
insights.quote: this moment is the first one that sits at the intersection of all of the forces that created the largest bubbles in US history

insights.claim: Overdetermined failure is the right model for expensive assets: roughly twenty independent 5%-probability failure paths compound to a greater than 60% chance of failure, so 'nobody can name the catalyst' is not evidence of safety.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Stop hunting for the single AI catalyst; size positions to the aggregate hazard rate implied by many small, independent failure modes.
insights.quote: At high valuations, failure is overdetermined in a statistical sense.

insights.claim: Nike's roughly 75% drawdown from its peak was driven mainly by multiple compression from about 70x to 20x earnings rather than by the product, competitive and political narratives that dominate public commentary - a warning that post-hoc stories systematically miss valuation as the cause.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber, host
insights.so_what: For richly valued AI names, the de-rating path can deliver most of the loss with no visible fundamental break, so waiting for bad news as a sell signal is too late.

insights.claim: As of the first half of 2026 more than half of data-center and hyperscaler financing comes from external sources - ABS, private credit, sovereigns and SPVs - rather than internal cash flow, reversing the exact argument bulls used to dismiss capex concerns.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: The AI trade is now a credit trade; monitor data-center ABS issuance and private-credit spreads as the leading indicator, not hyperscaler cash flow statements.
insights.quote: Now most of the financing as of mid 2026 is external financing coming from a constellation of things like ABS, private credit, sovereigns and everything else

insights.claim: Data-center-related paper is now roughly 15-18% of the investment-grade market per a JP Morgan report, making it a larger share than financial services would be as a sector.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Passive IG bond exposure is now a concentrated, undiagnosed bet on AI capex; investors holding IG index funds should measure their look-through data-center exposure.
insights.quote: something like 15 to 18% of the investment grade marketplace is now data center related

insights.claim: Lenders are underwriting data centers purely on the hyperscaler tenant's prime credit and a roughly 12-year renewable lease, with no diligence on the economics of what runs inside the building.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Credit demand is decoupled from AI unit economics, so overbuild continues until the tenant credit itself is questioned - watch hyperscaler credit ratings and lease guarantees as the true trigger.
insights.quote: there could be hideand go seek competitions going on inside the data centers and they wouldn't give a

insights.claim: Data-center borrowing is now crowding out sovereign issuance rather than the reverse, and contributed to the recent long-end bond selloff because investors prefer hyperscaler-backed paper to weak sovereign credits like the US or UK.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Long-end rate risk now has an AI-capex driver; a slowdown in data-center financing could be quietly bullish for duration.
insights.quote: It's much more appealing to loan to a data center and get a a hyperscaler with a prime credit implicitly or explicitly backing it than giving it to this flawed credit known as the United States

insights.claim: Debt-funded, perpetually-refreshed data centers turn technology companies into utility-like businesses with permanent maintenance capex, but they still trade at technology multiples rather than utility multiples.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: The re-rating is more likely to drag capex-heavy tech multiples down toward utilities than to lift utility multiples; a long-utilities / short-AI-capex-tech pair expresses the view.
insights.quote: In a sense, turning orthodox technology companies into a kind of utility company, right? With similar obligations, but wildly overvalued compared to an orthodox utility.

insights.claim: Tokens are the fastest-deflating commodity in modern economic history, falling roughly 70-80% a year, and the structural and technological reasons for that decline show no sign of reversing.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Any AI revenue model that assumes stable per-token pricing is mispriced; the durable value accrues to consumers and application layers, not to token sellers.
insights.quote: Tokens are the first hyper deflationary commodity in the history of of modern economies.

insights.claim: With prices falling about 80% a year, a frontier model company must grow units roughly 400% year-over-year merely to hold revenue flat - before satisfying Wall Street growth expectations or servicing newly external debt.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Use the 400% standstill hurdle as the yardstick for frontier-lab growth disclosures; anything below it is real contraction dressed as growth.
insights.quote: just just to stand still I need to grow 400% year-over-year

insights.claim: OpenAI's reported roughly 18% quarter-over-quarter growth in its most recent quarter was treated as a disappointment, illustrating how far expectations have detached from what the deflation math allows.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: The expectations gap for private AI labs is a setup for down-round or repricing risk in secondaries and pre-IPO marks.
insights.quote: OpenAI is apparently in it last quarter did 18% quarter after quarter, and that was deemed a disappointment.

insights.claim: AI's first successful domain - software - is uniquely unrepresentative of the rest of the economy because it has a tight grammar, rapid gradient descent, and is expansive (a short prompt yields a million lines of code) rather than compressive.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Token-demand projections extrapolated from coding workloads overstate future consumption because most white-collar uses shrink text rather than expand it.
insights.quote: the first domain where AI was applied could hardly be less representative of AI's future if you tried

insights.claim: AI's own buildout is a leading marginal contributor to emissions because grid interconnection cannot keep up and operators are adding behind-the-meter natural gas turbines, undercutting the industry's climate-solution pitch.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Behind-the-meter gas generation is a real demand stream for turbine and gas infrastructure suppliers, and a growing ESG and permitting liability for hyperscalers.
insights.quote: It's going to take a lot of AI to solve the problems created by AI in climate alone.

insights.claim: A narrow set of upcoming listings including SpaceX and Anthropic could bring roughly $5.5 trillion of new issuance - more than all US IPOs since World War II combined - after an earlier estimate of about $4 trillion.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: An equity supply shock of this scale is a market-wide de-rating risk independent of fundamentals; equity supply and issuance calendars deserve more weight than usual in 2026-27 allocation.
insights.quote: well not just that it's all post World War II combined

insights.claim: Long-only and index funds fund large IPO allocations by selling existing holdings, and they preferentially sell the most liquid, most correlated and best-performing names - so anticipated mega-IPOs pressure today's winners months in advance.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Crowded momentum leaders are the funding source for the IPO calendar; expect stealth distribution in them weeks to months before pricing dates.
insights.quote: The things that get sold tend to be the most liquid because I don't want to have a huge price impact.

insights.claim: Year-over-year gains on composite model benchmarks have essentially flatlined over the last six months, falling from 10-12% annual improvement to 1-2% at most, despite 18-month training cycles and billions of dollars of spend.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: If frontier gains are exhausted, the justification for the next training-run capex cycle collapses - the single most important variable for AI capex, GPU demand and data-center credit.
insights.quote: the year-over-year gains in the models themselves has essentially flatlined over the last 6 months

insights.claim: Model performance is not only flattening but converging, with little practical difference between frontier models from Anthropic, Qwen or DeepSeek in blind composite testing where users consistently fail to identify which is which.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Model quality is commoditizing, so pricing power and premium valuations for frontier labs are unsupportable; value shifts to distribution, harnesses and cost position.
insights.quote: There's there is very little difference between a frontier model from anthropic and a frontier model from Quen or from Deepseek

insights.claim: Published benchmark scores are effectively worthless because models ingest the benchmarks during training, and 'harnesses' such as Claude Code and Codex mask the underlying model plateau by making static models appear to improve rapidly.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Diligence on AI progress should track blind composite tests and harness-versus-model attribution, not vendor benchmark claims.
insights.quote: These are things like claude code and the codecs that wrap around the model and give the appearance of things changing much faster than they are.

insights.claim: LLM outputs are homogenizing rather than diversifying behavior because the training data itself is homogeneous - the median data point behind a model approximates a 37-year-old male on Reddit - so AI will increase herding, not reduce it.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Widespread AI use raises correlation of decisions and crowding in markets, arguing for higher tail-risk assumptions rather than the diversification story being pitched.
insights.quote: the median data nugget inside of a large language model is a 37y old male on Reddit

insights.claim: Unprecedented cash inflows into Taiwanese and Chinese chip manufacturers point to a tsunami of semiconductor supply arriving in early 2028, landing on top of an existing overhang of hoarded, double- and triple-ordered GPUs running at only about 35-40% utilization, and once capacity is locked in, fixed-cost coverage forces product out the door and prices toward zero.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: The 2028 supply wave plus idle hoarded GPUs is a datable catalyst for de-risking or shorting memory and chip names into the peak of the super-cycle narrative.
insights.quote: once you lock in supply my friend, prices are going to zero

insights.claim: An inference ASIC startup called Edged completed initial design verification in 42 days versus a typical six to seven months and had its first design work, evidence that AI is now structurally compressing chip design because chip code sits in the LLM sweet spot.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: If design cycles collapse from months to weeks, the tribal-knowledge moat protecting incumbent chip designers erodes and new competing designs proliferate.

insights.claim: AI-assisted 'vibe chipping' will flood fabs with novel designs - including low-power chips running on-device LLMs inside things like security cameras - which will help prick the AI bubble by breaking the assumed GPU duopoly and semiconductor super-cycle narrative.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: The 'GPUs are a durable monopoly/duopoly' premium is the most vulnerable assumption in the AI trade; watch edge-inference ASIC tape-outs as the tell.
insights.quote: instead of having Vibe coding, we're going to have kind of vibe chipping

insights.claim: AI and data-center capex has accounted for more than 50% of US GDP growth and has persisted at a large share for six straight quarters, so policymakers crediting tariffs for that growth have a broken causal model and may take actions that prove consequentially negative.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Expect policy mistakes as the AI capex contribution rolls over and the true growth engine is revealed - a macro risk that is not in consensus forecasts.
insights.quote: Your tariffs did not cause the US GDP to grow in that period.

insights.claim: American hostility to AI is anomalous versus other G7 and OECD countries - and far higher than in Sub-Saharan Africa and developing markets, where AI is seen as a leg up - largely because US health care is tied to employment, so job-loss messaging from AI leaders reads as a threat to personal solvency.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: US-specific political and regulatory backlash risk to AI is structurally higher than elsewhere, which matters for siting, permitting and policy exposure in domestic AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: any threat to employment is a threat to health care and a threat to health care is a threat to fiscal so your personal solveny

insights.claim: Roughly 75% of surveyed Americans say they would not want a data center in their county - a higher rejection rate than for nuclear - and the driver is a felt loss of personal agency rather than a fixable public-relations gap, so better messaging will not resolve it.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber, host, with Paul Kedrosky's interpretation
insights.so_what: Local siting opposition is an underpriced constraint on data-center buildout timelines and a cost driver for developers and the lenders underwriting their leases.
